user.name: Scott
user.biography: Scott Murray is Emeritus Professor of Primary Palliative Care. Through his research based in Family Practice, Professor Murray and his team have demonstrated the vital role of primary care in delivering palliative care early in the course of illness, across all diagnoses, and in addressing all dimensions of need.

data.title: TS: How well do we enable people to live fully until they die?
data.description:
Research into Rehabilitation in Palliative Care.

1) What we mean by 'Living fully until you die' and why it matters is appraised through diverse lenses from person to population:
- ‘What matters most’: a research synthesis on priorities of people living with palliative diagnoses - invites audience reflection
- ‘The disability pandemic’: an interrogation of the impact of cancer, advanced chronic illness, multimorbidity, ageing and frailty on function, independence, care needs and costs - sets the context for rehabilitation as a solution.
2) Cutting-edge research and practice examples from high, middle and low-income countries illustrate the value of rehabilitation in palliative care and how to integrate it to enable people to live fully until they die:
- ‘Rehabilitation is everybody’s business’: towards a consensus definition and shared understanding- ‘From contradiction to evidence-based best practice’: history and literature- ‘A radical culture shift’ an integrated rehabilitative, palliative and geriatric approach for older people living with frailty.

Aim and learning objectives:

To challenge participants to consider how well they enable people with advanced, serious illness, old age or frailty to live fully until they die – critically interrogating what we mean by this founding aspiration of palliative care and how it is realised and evaluated in practice and research.
To expand participants' understanding of rehabilitation in palliative care as an integrated approach to enable people to live fully until they die through a compelling synthesis of research, innovative examples, international recommendations and an interactive expert panel discussion.

data.title: Driving System Change in Palliative Care: A Collaborative Approach

schedule_event_manual_content.title: Driving System Change in Palliative Care: A Collaborative Approach
schedule_event_manual_content.summary:
This session will showcase examples of strategic, system-oriented projects carried out in the Czech Republic through collaboration between the Abakus Foundation, the Czech Society for Palliative Medicine, and other local organizations. The shared goal of these initiatives has been to improve access to and the quality of palliative care at the national level.

Developing Palliative Care Infrastructure in Hospitals (Presenter: Martin Loučka)

Although the majority of people in the Czech Republic die in hospitals, a decade ago there were virtually no palliative care teams in these settings. In response, the Abakus Foundation launched a nationwide programme involving 25 hospitals, providing both financial and methodological support to establish inpatient palliative care services. This initiative represented a groundbreaking innovation within the national health system, leading to the creation of a previously unavailable model of care. It also laid the groundwork for a follow-up project in cooperation with the Ministry of Health, aimed at ensuring the long-term sustainability and financing of this segment of care. The programme received the UN Sustainable Development Goals Award in recognition of its contribution to global health objectives, and the Abakus Foundation continues to support the established teams through other recent programmes.


Implementation of Palliative Care in Nursing Homes (Presenter: Matěj Lejsal)

This project focused on integrating palliative care principles into Czech nursing homes, where approximately 15,000 residents die each year. Two cohorts, comprising a total of 30 nursing homes, participated in a two-year implementation programme. The project involved developing clinical guidelines, tools for advance care planning, and building collaboration with specialized palliative care teams. A new role—the palliative care coordinator—was introduced as part of the programme and sustained by stakeholders and facility management even after the pilot phase ended. Multiple indicators were monitored to evaluate the programme’s impact, including the rate of terminal hospitalizations, which decreased by 30% across participating facilities during the programme.

Innovation through Collaboration

The session will conclude with a panel discussion on how to build effective collaboration among academia, the private sector, government institutions, NGOs, and care providers. The discussion will explore how to harness synergy across sectors to expand access to palliative care effectively and efficiently.

Moderator: Martin Loučka

Panelists: Matěj Lejsal, Sue Ryder, Prague, CZ; Ondřej Kopecký, President of the Czech Society for Palliative Medicine; Hana Benešová, Czech Ministry of Health; Přemysl Filip, Abakus Foundation; Joanne Brennan, EAPC

data.title: EAPC groups: Maximising the inclusivity of the public health approach to bereavement
data.description:
This session focuses on the research-based public health model for bereavement care. It poses questions for discussion on the translation of bereavement research into policy and practice, and more specifically, on implications for bereavement care for minoritised communities, including cultural and faith-based communities, those in prisons, the LGBTQI community, and people who are homeless.
Session one is an initial overview of the public health model for bereavement care, compassionate communities and associated evidence. Session two is a data-driven case study on how the public health model is implemented in a large urban hospital setting, and session three outlines policy and practice implementation examples on how bereavement care is managed and rolled out through a range of marginalised settings. 

Three EAPC taskforces/reference groups will be represented: the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. 

Session aim:
To explore a critical approach to the implementation of the public health bereavement model: integrating bereavement knowledge into practice for the benefit of all communities.  

Learning objectives:
• Integrate bereavement approaches across relevant task forces and reference groups at EAPC, including the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group.
• Identify the evidence base for an inclusive public health approach to bereavement care
• Appraise the challenges and opportunities for translating bereavement research evidence into practice for all communities, including seldom heard and minority groups


Speakers:

Prof Samar Aoun, Perron Institute Research Chair in Palliative Care, The University of Western Australia. EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. PRE-REC
Dr Steve Marshall, King’s College Hospital and King’s College London EAPC Social Work Taskforce
Prof Audrey Roulston, Queen's University Belfast, Co-Chair EAPC Social Work Taskforce
Irene Murphy and Orla Keegan, Co-Chairs EAPC Bereavement Taskforce

data.title: TS: Towards gold-standard methods in paediatric palliative care research, sharing knowledge, assessing challenges and opportunities.
data.description:
Research into Paediatric Palliative Care.

Effective delivery and adequate resourcing of healthcare rely on high-quality evidence to drive decisions. To date, PPC research has largely comprised small cohort studies (case studies, chart reviews, etc.).

Session aim:

Explore opportunities and challenges in applying best-practice research methods to PPC research, through knowledge sharing across multiple disciplines, thereby strengthening the evidence base on which PPC delivery, resourcing, and planning decisions are made.

Learning objectives:

Developing understanding and awareness of:- opportunities for engaging with children and families in research- real/perceived challenges in applying robust evaluation techniques in PPC (e.g., randomised controlled trials)- methods for population-level planning of PPC.

The session will comprise three short presentations followed by structured discussion time.
Presentation 1 will focus on the increasingly vital role of Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) in health services research, specifically highlighting the engagement of children and young people (CYP). Prof Veronica Lambert will chart the evidence on CYP involvement as active PPI contributors across all stages of the PPC research cycle.
Presentation 2 will examine real/perceived challenges to conducting randomised controlled trials and other robust evaluation techniques in PPC research. Prof Lorna Fraser will demonstrate the availability of core building blocks required for measuring effectiveness and cost effectiveness in PPC and discuss challenges and opportunities for advancing methods further.
Presentation 3 will highlight recent learnings from national level analysis on planning for PPC. Dr Samantha Smith will discuss challenges in defining need for PPC at a population-level, incorporating markers of complexity and applicability of methods to different data sources.

data.title: EAPC Partnered Research
data.description:
Chaired by Patricia White and Tamara Radojicic (Pal-Cycles)

Panel 1: Recruitment, equity and inclusion in trials

This panel will explore how equity, inclusion and diversity can be embedded across study design, consortium governance, implementation and dissemination, with attention to structural inequities in access, inclusive recruitment, culturally and linguistically appropriate methods, and equitable partnership models. The session will highlight practical strategies and measurable indicators.

Panellists: Lise Nottleman (INSPIRE), Everlien de Graaf (RAPHAEL), Manuel Luís Vila Capelas (Pal-Cycles), Nicola Cornally (In Touch)

Panel 2: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in palliative care research

This panel will examine how AI can be responsibly integrated into research projects to enhance communication training, personalise care planning, support clinical decision-making, and generate real-world evidence, while addressing risks such as algorithmic bias, data governance, and digital exclusion.

Panellists: Izidor Mlakar (AI4HOPE), Alexander Varjord (INSPIRE), Jan Hrdlička (VR Talks), Carsten Klein

data.title: EAPC Groups: Palliative oxygen therapy: preliminary guidelines and reconsideration within the palliative care continuum
data.description:
This session is planned to discuss clinical guidelines regarding palliative oxygen therapy. These guidelines are generated by the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy and regard POT definition, outcome measures follow up and regimens. This task force was developed in recognition of the need to support the use of palliative oxygen therapy. Currently, its use is limited due to a lack of a consensual definition, due to unclear eligibility, limited evidence supporting various regimens (low flow versus high flow therapy) and the lack of validated outcome measures. We established several working groups within this Task Force and tried to gather and analyse the existing evidence on the above mentioned issues. Some of the evidence is generated via systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature, and some other is generated based on consensus elicited via the Delphi procedure. For both categories, it would be very useful to have an interactive exchange of opinions before wrapping everything up and drafting the clinical guideline paper.

Questions and learning objectives:  

How should palliative oxygen therapy be defined?
Should low-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT?
Should high-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT?
What are the eligibility criteria for palliative oxygen therapy?
How should palliative oxygen therapy be administered and followed up?

Speakers:

Prof Sabina Antoniu, University of Medicine and Pharmacy Grigore T Popa Iasi, Romania 

Prof Magnus Ekström, Lund University, Sweden

Dr Slavica Kochovska, Flinders University Adelaide, Australia

Dr Filip Bjorklund, Lund University, Sweden

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy.

data.title: TS: Methodological approaches to research into requests for assisted dying: added value & challenges
data.description:
Research into Requests for Assisted Dying.

In this themed session, participants will engage with diverse research on requests for assisted dying in palliative care, conducted using distinct methodologies and situated in different countries and contexts. The main emphasis will be on the employed methodologies, examining the novelty and added value of each approach in uncovering relevant insights, as well as the challenges and pitfalls they present in data collection and analysis. Through a rich and in-depth group interaction process, participants will leave the session with a range of recommendations for further research and practice.

Content of the session:

- Short introduction to the session
- Three concise presentations on research into requests for assisted dying, which, next to sharing the main findings, will focus on the methodologies used, their added value, and the complexities encountered. Each contribution will centre on a distinct methodological approach:
1) international comparative research;
2) qualitative ethnographic approaches;
3) consensus-building methods
- a moderated group discussion on issues related to doing research on assisted dying (and its relationship to palliative care).

data.title: EAPC Partnered Research
data.description:
Chaired by Fódhla Ní Chéileachair (EAPC) and Everlien de Graaf (RAPHAEL)

Panel 3: Issues with implementation

This panel will explore barriers such as regulatory variation, workforce capacity, cultural differences, integration into routine care, sustainability beyond project funding, and uneven adoption across countries. The session will identify practical strategies from implementation science to enhance scalability, long-term impact, and real-world uptake of palliative care innovations across Europe.

Panellists: Elias Lundereng (MyPath), Lieve van den Block (EuNavigate), Sergi Navaro (PALLIAKID), Suzanne Timmons (IN TOUCH and AI4Hope)

Panel 4: Moving research into practice

This panel will examine the gap between evidence generation and real-world adoption, exploring knowledge translation strategies, stakeholder engagement and sustainable service integration across diverse European health systems. The session will highlight practical models and success factors that enable research findings to influence clinical practice and organisational change at scale.

Panellists: Katrine Rolid (EUonQOL, JANE2), Roman Rolke (RAPHAEL), Ulf Bremberg (PsyPal), Jo Bayly (INSPIRE)

data.title: EAPC Groups: Palliative Care Meets Emergency Medical Services. An International Call to Action
data.description:
The integration of palliative care into out-of-hospital emergency services is gaining momentum worldwide. People with life-limiting illnesses often face acute medical emergencies, which, in the absence of clear communication and structural pathways, may lead to distressing overtreatment from emergency care workers. This session presents experiences from South Africa, Australia and Germany on systematically strengthening palliative care within EMS — from provider and patient surveys to concrete implementation concepts, in addition to an overview of the state of palliative paramedicine affairs globally. Building on these insights, a proposal for a European White Paper will be introduced. The session aims to foster international exchange and develop joint recommendations for improving palliative care in EMS across Europe and further abroad.

The aims and learning objectives:

- Understand the unique role of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) in delivering palliative care. 
- Explore how integrating palliative care benefits EMS, palliative care services, patient outcomes and the broader healthcare system, through a global systems lens.
- Learn from international models, including South Africa (low-to-middle income country context), Australia and Germany. 
- Identify key elements for implementation such as communication, documentation, education and policy.
- Reflect on how these insights can inform local practice and support a European framework.

Speakers:

Dr Caleb Gage, Paramedic, University of Cape Town, South Africa, 
Dr Eva Diehl-Wiesenecker, Consultant Emergency Medicine, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany; Department of Palliative Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Augsburg, Germany
Ms Georgina Murphy-Jones, Deputy Director of Clinical Assessment and Pathways at London Ambulance Service, UK
Dr Martin Loucka, Founder, Center for Palliative Care, Czech Republic
Ms Michala Chatrna, Project manager and researcher, Center for Palliative Care & Masaryk University, Brno, Czech Republic

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Care & Emergency Medical Services
